newsitem.title: FRANCE: France wants Europe to have a firm trade policy.
newsitem.headline: France wants Europe to have a firm trade policy.

text.p: French Industry Minister Franck Borotra said on Wednesday he wanted Europe to conduct a firm trade policy towards North America and east Asia to safeguard Europe's social conditions and jobs.
Without explicitly singling out the United States and Japan, Borotra said he wanted Europe to be "pragmatic, not dogmatic" in its approach towards the dollar and yen trading blocks.
But he told a New Year's reception that Europe should conduct a reciprocal tariff policy and not be lured into giving up advantages without getting anything in return.
Borotra, an indefatigable fighter for French interests, has broadened his horizons in 1997 beyond France to Europe.

"I believe that for Europe, the time of unilateral tariff concessions has now ended. The future of employment is too important for us to do that (make concessions) without a basis of reciprocity," he told reporters.
"Freedom of trade, yes, but freedom of trade on the basis of reciprocity," he added.

The European Union has been involved in trade disputes with both the United States and Japan. Fears that exports notably from east Asia will cost jobs in Europe, where structural unemployment is generally high, have strengthened the protectionist lobby.
"The differences in production costs and monetary parities are too important for us to renounce, when needed, the commercial weapons Europe has at its disposal," said Borotra.
Borotra said that European Monetary Union (EMU), scheduled to start in 1999, would be a useful tool.

"Questions about the parity between the franc and the mark make no economic sense at all today. The single currency is without a doubt the answer to power relationships with other blocks and competitive differences," he said.
"I hope that in its dealings with the other trading blocks, be it dollar or yen, Europe will be pragmatic and not dogmatic."
He brushed aside comments that he was interventionist and protectionist, saying that while he wanted Europe to adapt to market conditions, he wanted it do to so in a controlled way.
Borotra mentioned four areas that would have his particular attention in 1997, including the textile and clothing industry, which has been hit hard by cheaper imports.
The car sector was also a priority, as Europe's motor industry will face full competition in the year 2000 after import barriers are removed.
Borotra said the restructuring of the naval shipyards and the pharmaceutical industry also had his full attention.
Rumours have emerged on the stock market of possible mergers between a number of French pharmaceutical companies, although all involved have denied them.
